common_name: Chieftain Savoy Cabbage (1938 AAS-Winning Heirloom Savoy)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or sow in early-to-midsummer for a fall crop, since Chieftain reaches full size only in cool weather and improves in flavor after light frost.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost, or in early-to-midsummer for a fall crop, since Chieftain reaches full size only in cool weather and its flavor improves markedly after light frost. Chieftain Savoy is a 1938 All-America Selections winner bred by Ferry-Morse, producing large, nearly round, densely savoyed dark green heads averaging four to six pounds with a tender, sweet crunch that distinguishes savoy types from smooth-leaved cabbage. It is notably cold hardy and holds well in the garden into late fall and early winter, making it a dependable choice for extending the cabbage harvest well past the first frosts. Space plants generously to allow the broad, crinkled outer leaves to develop fully, and side-dress with nitrogen midseason to support the long growing period to a full-sized head.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, and again every few weeks through midsummer plus a late-summer fall sowing, since Kolibri matures quickly and mildest in cool weather.

directions: Direct sow seed ½ inch deep in early spring 2-4 weeks before the last frost, and again in mid- to late summer for a fall crop, since Kolibri grows fastest and mildest in cool weather. Kolibri is a widely grown F1 hybrid noted as one of the most uniform and reliably deep-purple kohlrabi varieties available, forming a smooth, round, above-ground bulb with crisp, nearly fiberless white flesh beneath the vivid purple skin. Its rapid 45- to 50-day maturity and compact, neat habit make it well suited to succession planting, small-space beds, and early-season cloche or row-cover production. Harvest bulbs at about the size of a tennis ball for the sweetest, most tender texture, since kohlrabi can turn woody if left too long in the ground.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants out 12-16 weeks ahead of the first fall frost so this long-season heirloom matures in cool weather and sweetens after frost.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants out roughly 12-16 weeks ahead of the first fall frost so the long-season crop matures in cool weather. Red Rubine is a Dutch open-pollinated heirloom dating to the mid-20th century, prized for its striking purple-red buttons and matching purple-veined foliage, a dramatic contrast to standard green Brussels sprouts. Its sprouts are smaller and yields somewhat lighter than modern green hybrids, but the flavor is rich and nutty and intensifies with sweetness after hard frost, and the purple color often persists lightly even after cooking. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making Red Rubine a favorite of heirloom seed savers and gardeners seeking ornamental as well as edible value in the fall garden.

common_name: Mei Qing Choi (Compact Hybrid Bok Choy)
scientific_name: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Mei Qing Choi'

planting.note: Direct sow, or start indoors and transplant, shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since Mei Qing Choi bolts quickly under long, hot days.

directions: Direct sow, or start indoors and transplant, in early spring after the last hard freeze, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since Mei Qing Choi bolts quickly in long, hot days. Mei Qing Choi is a compact, vase-shaped hybrid pac choi with thick, pale jade-green stems and glossy, rounded dark green leaves, bred for a uniform, tightly packed miniature head that is smaller and more tender than standard-sized bok choy. It combines useful heat and cold tolerance with strong bolt resistance for a bok choy of its type, giving gardeners a wider planting window than many other Asian brassica greens. Harvest whole heads at baby size for salads or at full size for stir-fries, cutting at the base just above the soil line.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension Asian Vegetables

planting.note: Direct sow shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Win-Win Choi's improved heat tolerance allows a somewhat longer planting window than many pac choi types.

directions: Direct sow in early spring after danger of hard frost has passed, or in late summer for a fall harvest, spacing seedlings close together for the miniature form Win-Win Choi is bred to produce. Win-Win Choi is a compact, white-stemmed hybrid pac choi that forms a bulky, uniform, vase-shaped head only about a foot tall at full size, making it well suited to close spacing, containers, and gardeners who prefer a smaller-format bok choy to the larger green-stemmed types. Its improved heat tolerance compared to many pac choi varieties allows for a longer planting window into warmer weather before bolting becomes a concern. Harvest whole plants at the baby stage for tender salad use or let them fill out for a heartier stir-fry green.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or sow in midsummer for a fall crop, since Kalibos develops its deepest color and best flavor with a longer, cooler growing season.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in midsummer for transplanting out in late summer, since Kalibos develops its best color and flavor with a longer, cooler fall growing season. Kalibos is a Central/Eastern European heirloom cabbage, likely developed from the older Vysoky (Vysocke) type, distinguished by small, dense, cone-shaped heads of deep purple-red leaves that form a striking pointed rosette rather than the round or flattened heads of typical cabbage. The tender, crisp, juicy leaves are deep red to violet clear through to the core, making Kalibos as prized for its color in raw slaws and pickles as for its mild, sweet flavor. It stores for a moderate period after harvest and remains something of a novelty in North American gardens despite long popularity in Eastern Europe.

common_name: Des Vertus Savoy Cabbage (French Heirloom Drumhead Savoy)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a summer harvest, or sow in early summer for a fall crop; Des Vertus holds especially well and even overwinters in mild climates.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost for a summer harvest, or sow in early summer for transplanting out for a fall crop, since Des Vertus develops its full flavor and holds especially well after cool autumn weather sets in. Des Vertus Savoy, also known as Large Drumhead Savoy, is a French heirloom cabbage dating to the early 1800s that produces large, rounded, medium-green heads of four to six pounds with deeply crinkled, blistered savoy-type leaves. Its flavor is notably mild, sweet, and tender compared to smooth-leaved cabbage, and the crinkled leaves make it a traditional choice for stuffed cabbage preparations across French and other European cuisines. It is more cold-tolerant than many cabbages, standing well into fall and even overwintering in mild climates, and offers moderate storage life once harvested.

common_name: Golden Frills Mustard (Frilled Gold Salad Green)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; spring sowings are more prone to flea beetle damage than late-summer ones.

directions: Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop, since Golden Frills grows best in the cool temperatures of spring and autumn and can suffer flea beetle damage in warm weather. Golden Frills is a strikingly ornamental mustard green with finely dissected, deeply lobed, chartreuse-gold leaves that add texture and bright color to salad mixes and cut-and-come-again plantings. Its flavor is sweet and aromatic with a mustard bite that is milder than many mustard greens, and mature plants sometimes develop a crisp, edible root reflecting a mustard-turnip heritage in its lineage. Harvest young for baby leaf salads at around three weeks, or allow plants to grow to full size for a spicier, more robust cooking green.
